newsitem.title: USA: U.S. talks cooperation, not confrontation with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. talks cooperation, not confrontation with China.

text.p: The United States Tuesday talked up cooperation with China and played down confrontation ahead of a meeting of leaders of the two countries next week.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters after a two-day meeting of the U.S.-China Joint Economic Committee that bilateral differences on specific issues were inevitable, but that they should not be allowed to colour overall ties.

"Two large nations, such as China and the United States ... will inevitably have disagreements over specific issues," he said. "The key is not to let individual disagreements affect the overall relationship."
Rubin's comments were the latest in a series by U.S. officials aimed at repairing once-frayed relations with the giant Asian nation.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, en route to Beijing for high-level talks, told reporters Tuesday that China's jailing of prominent dissident Wang Dan will not be an impediment to U.S.-Chinese summits.
"I'd emphasise the importance of the overall relationship, the fact that we need to have a steady and comprehensive approach to the relationship that's not rooted in a single issue," he said.
Christopher's trip is a prelude to a meeting Sunday between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin on the fringes of a gathering of leaders from Asia-Pacific nations.
Rubin called this week's gathering of the U.S.-China Joint Economic Committee "highly valuable" and suggested that the two sides might meet again toward the end of next year in Beijing.
The talks in Washington covered a wide range of issues, from China's alleged abuses of human rights of its citizens to the openness of its financial markets to foreigners.

In a joint statement issued after their meeting, Rubin and Chinese Finance Minister Liu Zhongli unveiled a series of minor steps aimed at fostering economic cooperation between the two nations in the tax, securities and financial arenas.

Separately, the U.S. government-owned Export-Import Bank announced it had approved $792 million in financing for the export of U.S. equipment and services to two power projects in China. San Francisco-based Bechtel Corp. and Foster Wheeler Corp. of Clinton, N.J., were the two U.S. companies to benefit from the export financimg.
Both Rubin and Liu also cast a positive light on perhaps the most vexing economic issue separating the two sides now: Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
"We believe there has been a constructive atmosphere," Rubin said, commenting on talks between the two nations on the WTO membership bid. But, he added, "There is a lot of work to do."
For his part, Liu, speaking through an interpreter, took note of what he called the "flexible and pragmatic" attitude of the U.S. toward Chinse membership in the WTO.
China in the past has accused the United States of blocking its entry to the WTO, charging Washington has set too high a standard for Beijing's membership in the world trade body.
The two sides discussed, but did not negotiate, the membership question during their Washington talks.
All was not sweetness and light, however.

Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, who heads the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, Tuesday warned the Clinton administration against speeding up China's entry into the WTO without consulting Congress first.

In a letter to Christopher, the combative North Carolina lawmaker said that China's repeated violations of textile agreements with the United States raised questions about its bid to join the organisation that sets world trade rules and hears disputes. Several U.S. textile companies have operations in North Carolina.

Asked for specific ways in which the United States could promote stability across the Taiwan Strait, Qian referred to the 1982 Sino-U.S. communique pledging a reduction and eventual termination of American arms sales to Taiwan.
"We can only feel reassured when this promise is turned into reality," Qian said.
Qian also said that ties between the two nations had taken a turn for the better despite disagreements over Taiwan, arms sales, trade and human rights.
Christopher arrived in Beijing on Tuesday for his first visit to China in two years.
